description.value: The study used event-related fMRI to examine neural responses to smoking-related, neutral, and rare target images in nicotine-deprived smokers and nonsmoking comparison participants.

spans.text: Event-related functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) was used to detect brain activation after exposure to smoking-related images in a group of nicotine-deprived smokers and a nonsmoking comparison group.

value: we hypothesized that two distinct neural circuits might be activated by smoking cues: a reward circuit identified by animal studies of drug reinforcement and a visuospatial attention circuit identified by human functional imaging studies.
We therefore postulated that visual smoking cues would activate these areas preferentially in nicotine-deprived smokers.

value: For smokers, smoking-related images elicited significantly greater activation than neutral images in the posterior fusiform gyrus, intraparietal sulcus, posterior hippocampus, medial thalamus, ventral tegmental area, posterior amygdala, inferior frontal gyrus, middle frontal gyrus, and nucleus accumbens.

These findings indicate that mesocorticolimbic circuits may be activated by salient drug-related stimuli alone, without drug ingestion or its associated reward, and that smoking cues elicit a pattern of active brain regions associated with visuospatial attention.
